clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive congenital myopathy caused by MTM1 mutations encoding myotubularin, a phosphoinositide phosphatase regulating membrane trafficking and excitation-contraction coupling.
Affected male neonates present with profound hypotonia, respiratory failure frequently requiring immediate ventilatory support, and feeding difficulty.
Macrocephaly, a long face, external ophthalmoplegia and undescended testes are characteristic supportive features.
Muscle biopsy shows small rounded fibres with central nuclei resembling fetal myotubes, with central aggregation of oxidative enzyme activity on NADH and SDH staining.
Antenatal clues include polyhydramnios, reduced fetal movements and increased birth length.
Female carriers are usually asymptomatic but may show variable weakness through skewed X-inactivation.
Milder and later-onset MTM1 phenotypes are increasingly recognised and should not be excluded by survival beyond infancy.
Belongs to the centronuclear myopathy family alongside autosomal DNM2- and BIN1-related forms.
reference.pathophysiology: MTM1 encodes myotubularin, a lipid phosphatase that dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate and its 3,5-bisphosphate, regulating endosomal membrane trafficking, autophagy and the triad structures responsible for excitation-contraction coupling. Loss of function disorganises T-tubules and triad positioning, impairs calcium release and arrests myofibre maturation, so nuclei persist centrally in a manner reminiscent of fetal myotubes and severe congenital weakness results.
additionalInvestigations: MTM1 sequencing with deletion and duplication analysis
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry (NADH, SDH, PAS)
Serum creatine kinase (usually normal or mildly raised)
Overnight oximetry and capnography with respiratory function assessment
Cranial and muscle imaging where indicated
Genetic counselling and carrier testing of the mother
redFlags: Hepatic peliosis or haemorrhage, a recognised MTM1 association
reference.prognosis: Classic severe disease historically carries high early mortality from respiratory failure, although survival is improving with ventilatory and nutritional support and milder variants run a more favourable course. Gene-directed therapies are under active investigation.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal hypotonia solely to central causes and missing a primary myopathy.
Being falsely reassured by a normal creatine kinase.
Overlooking hepatic haemorrhage or peliosis as a cause of sudden deterioration.
Failing to test and counsel the carrier mother and at-risk female relatives.
Assuming survival beyond infancy excludes an MTM1 diagnosis.
references: Dubowitz V, Sewry CA, Oldfors A. Muscle Biopsy: A Practical Approach
International consensus guidance on the congenital myopathies
management: Provide ventilatory support as the mainstay, with neonatal invasive or non-invasive ventilation and early consideration of tracheostomy for chronic ventilator dependence
Secure nutrition through nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding to overcome bulbar weakness and reduce aspiration risk
Offer physiotherapy, orthoses, contracture prevention and adaptive equipment to optimise residual motor function
Enrol in specialist neuromuscular follow-up and consider emerging MTM1 gene-directed (AAV-myotubularin) therapy through clinical trials
Undertake surveillance for known complications, notably hepatic peliosis and life-threatening hepatic haemorrhage, cryptorchidism and progressive respiratory decline
Offer genetic counselling and carrier testing for the mother and at-risk female relatives, with antenatal or preimplantation options given X-linked inheritance
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, respiratory, gastroenterology, orthopaedics and palliative medicine, with advance-care planning in severe disease
